title: ⭐ Practice: one structure at a time

questions.prompt: Complete: "My grandmother never lets ___ leave without a glass of tea."
questions.explanation: The word that follows let is an object pronoun, so the sentence takes "us": lets us leave. "we" is the subject pronoun and can only stand in front of its own verb, as in we leave early. "our" is the possessive and must be followed by a noun, as in our house. "ourselves" is the reflexive and would say that we give ourselves the permission, when the sentence says the grandmother gives it.

questions.prompt: Complete: "If a teenager ___ his parents shouting every evening, he stops telling them anything."
questions.explanation: This structure keeps a present tense in both halves, and the subject a teenager is singular, so the if-clause takes "hears". "will hear" puts a future inside an if-clause, which English never allows. "would hear" moves the first half into the imaginary while the second half, he stops, stays in the present, so the two halves no longer match. "hearing" is not a tense and would need an auxiliary in front of it.

questions.prompt: Three of these words hide a letter that is written but never pronounced. Which one hides none?
questions.explanation: "husband" is the one: all seven of its letters are pronounced, one after the other. "whistle" hides its t, which disappears between the s and the le, exactly as in castle. "doubt" hides its b, which is written and never said. "wrong" hides its w, like write and wrist.

questions.prompt: Your classmate is in the middle of a long speech and you want to say one thing before she goes on. Which phrase do you use?

options.text: I don't agree at all with that point.
As far as I am concerned, she is right.
Could I stop you here for a moment?
I just wish somebody would listen to me.

questions.explanation: Interrupting politely means asking for the floor with a question, so the phrase is "Could I stop you here for a moment?" "I don't agree at all with that point." expresses disagreement, which you can only do once you already have the floor. "As far as I am concerned, she is right." opens an opinion rather than asking to speak. "I just wish somebody would listen to me." is a complaint about your own situation, and a complaint is not a request for a turn.

questions.prompt: Read: "Sami noticed that his grandmother was cold and brought her a blanket without being asked." Which adjective, built on the noun thought, describes him?
questions.explanation: The suffix -ful builds "thoughtful", the adjective for somebody who thinks of other people's needs, which is exactly what noticing the cold and fetching a blanket shows. "thoughtless" is built with -less and says the opposite: that he never thinks of anybody. "thoughtfully" is the adverb in -ly and would have to follow a verb — he acted thoughtfully — not describe a person after is. "thinkable" is built on the verb think, not on the noun thought, and it means possible to imagine — which says nothing about caring for anyone.

questions.prompt: Which line gives three words of the same family, all of them correctly formed?
questions.explanation: Only reassure — reassurance — reassuring is built throughout: -ance turns the verb into a noun, and -ing turns it into an adjective describing what the thing does to you. In "expect — expectation — expectful" the noun is right but expectful does not exist; the adjective English uses here is expectant. In "frustrate — frustratation — frustrated" the adjective is right, but the noun doubles a syllable that is not there: it is frustration. In "nurture — nurturement — nurturing" the adjective is right, but nurturement is not a word: the noun English builds here is nurturance — the very name of the family role you learnt — and nurture is itself already a noun.
